plot_or_argument: The book alternates between prose chapters arguing for the primacy of the imagination and short poems that demonstrate it — 'By the road to the contagious hospital', 'The Red Wheelbarrow', 'To Elsie', 'Spring and All' — and ends with the declaration that the imagination is the only reality.
narrative_structure: Twenty-seven sections alternating prose chapters and poems. A collection of short separate poems, each built on one image or one cadence, standing alone rather than forming a continuous narrative.
principal_characters: Elsie, the girl of 'The pure products of America' ('To Elsie')
literary_form: Poetry collection with prose (published in Paris by Contact Editions)
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Free verse in the imagist manner: the unrhymed cadenced line, the hard exact image, the omission of the connecting argument and the refusal of the received stanza, with the rhythm of the phrase rather than the metronome. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the line measured by the breath and broken by speech.
historical_context: The New Jersey of Williams's medical practice, the Armory Show and the new American art of the 1910s, and the Imagist and Dadaist movements. The record dates the work as composed between 1922 and 1923 and first published in 1923 and the corpus places it within American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric; Imagism and the Free-Verse Revolution, it is catalogued under imagist lyric and the free-verse line; modernist lyric and the new idiom.
literary_significance: Spring and All is the most radical American book of the period: its mixture of manifesto and poem, its plain American idiom and its insistence on things made it the founding text of the American objectivist tradition, and 'The Red Wheelbarrow' is the most discussed short poem in American literature.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Contact Publishing in Paris in May 1923 in an edition of some 300 copies; the William Carlos Williams volume of 1944 collects it with the poems of 1935-39. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Paterson
description: The great American long poem of place: a New Jersey city, a doctor, and the search for a language in which things can be said. It is a verse work of 1946 by William Carlos Williams; it belongs to American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric and it is catalogued here under modernist long poem and the mythical method and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: The poem follows the city of Paterson and its river, its falls and its people, and the figure of the doctor-poet who walks it; it assembles letters, documents, newspaper cuttings and lyric passages into a single work about the American place and the American idiom.
narrative_structure: Five books, each in three parts, mixing lyric, letter and document. A long poem built as a sequence of fragments in several voices, ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative sequence.
principal_characters: The doctor; Paterson; the river; the falls
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the modernist long poem: the polyphonic sequence of fragments in free verse and in borrowed metres, quotation and allusion doing the work of connective argument, the whole ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative. The author's characteristic manner is the line measured by the breath and broken by speech.
historical_context: The industrial city of Paterson, New Jersey, and its history; the America of the 1940s and 1950s; and Williams's own medical practice among its people. The record dates the work as composed between 1944 and 1958 and first published in 1946 and the corpus places it within American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric, it is catalogued under modernist long poem and the mythical method.
literary_significance: Paterson is the great American long poem after The Waste Land and the founding work of the American objectivist epic: it made a single American city the subject of a modernist long poem.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Book I was published by New Directions in Norfolk, Connecticut, in May 1946; Book II in 1948, Book III in 1949, Book IV in 1951, and the posthumous Book V by New Directions in 1958, the whole issued by Jonathan Cape in London in 1963. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Poems (Moore, 1921)
description: Moore's first collection, published by her friends: the syllabic stanza, the menagerie and the exact eye. It is a verse work of 1921 by Marianne Moore; it belongs to American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric and it is catalogued here under modernist lyric and the new idiom and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: The collection — published by the Egoist Press in London — contains 'The Fish', 'A Grave', 'Poetry', 'To a Steam Roller' and 'The Monkeys', the poems that established her syllabic stanza and exact zoological observation.
narrative_structure: Twenty-four poems in syllabic stanzas with internal rhyme. A collection of separate poems rather than a continuous narrative; the pieces stand alone and are commonly read individually.
literary_form: Poetry collection (published by H.D. and Bryher without the poet's knowledge)
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the syllabic stanza counted by syllables and not by stress.

title: Observations
description: Moore's second collection, the one that made her reputation: 'The Fish', 'A Grave', 'Poetry' and the syllabic stanza perfected. It is a verse work of 1924 by Marianne Moore; it belongs to American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric and it is catalogued here under modernist lyric and the new idiom.

narrative_structure: Fifty-three poems in syllabic stanzas. A collection of separate poems rather than a continuous narrative; the pieces stand alone and are commonly read individually.
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the syllabic stanza counted by syllables and not by stress.

title: Tulips and Chimneys
description: Cummings's first collection: the typographic lyric, the love poem and the satire of the modern state. It is a verse work of 1923 by e e cummings; it belongs to American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric and it is catalogued here under modernist lyric and the new idiom.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'in Just-spring', 'the Cambridge ladies who live in furnished souls', 'Thy fingers make early flowers of', 'Buffalo Bill's defunct' and 'next to of course god america i' — love lyrics, satires and the first full display of Cummings's typographic method.
narrative_structure: Seventy-three poems, including sonnets, songs and typographic experiments. A collection of separate poems rather than a continuous narrative; the pieces stand alone and are commonly read individually.
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the typographic page as a compositional unit.
historical_context: The Cambridge and Greenwich Village of the 1910s, the First World War, and the new art movements of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1919 and 1923 and first published in 1923 and the corpus places it within American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric, it is catalogued under modernist lyric and the new idiom.
literary_significance: Tulips and Chimneys introduced the typographic poem to English and established Cummings as the most popular experimental poet of the century: its lowercase 'i', its broken words and its parenthesis made the printed page part of the poem.

title: The Bridge
description: The great American epic of the Brooklyn Bridge: the myth of America, the machine and the poetic imagination. It is a verse work of 1930 by Hart Crane; it belongs to The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method and it is catalogued here under modernist long poem and the mythical method and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: The poem begins with 'Proem: To Brooklyn Bridge' and moves through Columbus, Pocahontas, the subway, the Mississippi riverboat, the tramp, the sailor and the film comedians, ending with 'Atlantis' and a vision of the bridge as the symbol of American possibility and of the poet's own aspiration.
narrative_structure: Fifteen sections in a symphonic structure, from 'Ave Maria' to 'Atlantis'. A long poem built as a sequence of fragments in several voices, ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative sequence.
principal_characters: Columbus; Pocahontas; Rip Van Winkle; the sailor; the poet
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the modernist long poem: the polyphonic sequence of fragments in free verse and in borrowed metres, quotation and allusion doing the work of connective argument, the whole ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative. The author's characteristic manner is the dense, prophetic, syntactically compressed lyric.
historical_context: The Brooklyn Bridge, New York in the 1920s, the American past from Columbus to the frontier, and Crane's reading of Whitman and Eliot. The record dates the work as composed between 1923 and 1929 and first published in 1930 and the corpus places it within The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method; American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric, it is catalogued under modernist long poem and the mythical method.
literary_significance: The Bridge is the great American epic poem of the period and the most ambitious answer to The Waste Land: it attempted to give America a mythic poem of its own, and its fusion of the machine, the past and the imagination made it the most beautiful long poem of American modernism.

title: 1914 and Other Poems
description: The five 1914 sonnets and the Georgian lyrics of the poet who became the emblem of the war's first year. It is a verse work of 1915 by Rupert Brooke; it belongs to Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric and it is catalogued here under georgian anthology lyric; trench lyric and the war poem.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains the five war sonnets of 1914 — 'Peace', 'Safety', 'The Dead' (two), 'The Soldier' — together with the earlier Georgian lyrics, 'The Old Vicarage, Grantchester', 'The Great Lover' and the South Seas poems.
narrative_structure: A posthumous collection of lyrics and the five war sonnets. A collection of separate short poems in the anthology manner, ordered by subject rather than by narrative. A sequence of separate lyrics, each a single moment of the war, to be read in the order in which the collection sets them.
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the Georgian lyric manner: the rhymed stanza of four or eight lines, the plain monosyllabic diction, the observed countryside and the elegiac undertone, without the modernist break in syntax. The text was published posthumously, from the manuscript or from the papers left at the author's death. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the Georgian sonnet and the rhymed lyric.
historical_context: The first year of the First World War, Brooke's service with the Royal Naval Division, and his death on the hospital ship off Skyros in April 1915, which made the book a national event. The record dates the work as composed in 1914 and first published in 1915 and the corpus places it within Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric; Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War, it is catalogued under georgian anthology lyric; trench lyric and the war poem.
literary_significance: 1914 and Other Poems gave the war its rhetoric of sacrifice: 'The Soldier' — 'some corner of a foreign field / That is for ever England' — is one of the most famous English poems of the century, and the book's posthumous publication made Brooke the myth of the golden generation.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Rupert Chawner Brooke. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Sidgwick and Jackson in May 1915; the poet died at Skyros on 23 April 1915 and the collection became the best-selling volume of verse of the war years. The record grades the work as secondary canon.
